extracted.intended_audience: students, policymakers, and readers of political economy (legislators, tax designers, economists)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length treatment of principles for designing and evaluating public revenue and taxes, especially land taxation — sets out general maxims for taxation and detailed criteria for land-tax administration and revenue sources. Useful for assessing tax fairness, certainty, convenience, administrative cost, and economic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution proportionate to ability (equality of taxation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjects of every state ought to contribute towards the support of the government, as nearly as possible, in proportion to their respective abilities; that is, in proportion to the revenue which they respectively enjoy under the protection of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim grounds the notion of equality in taxation. The chapter notes rent, profit, and wages as the three ultimate private revenue sources and observes that any tax falling finally on only one of them is necessarily unequal relative to the others. The author focuses on inequality caused by particular taxes falling unevenly upon the specific fund they affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes ought to be certain and not arbitrary (certainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tax which each individual is bound to pay, ought to be certain and not arbitrary. The time of payment, the manner of payment, the quantity to be paid, ought all to be clear and plain to the contributor, and to every other person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uncertainty in taxation empowers tax-gatherers to aggravate taxes or extort perquisites, encouraging insolence and corruption. The chapter argues that some inequality is less harmful than uncertainty; certainty is a matter of great importance in taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes should be convenient for the contributor (convenience/timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tax ought to be levied at the time, or in the manner, in which it is most likely to be convenient for the contributor to pay it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tax on rent payable when rents are usually paid; taxes on luxury consumables paid gradually by consumers as purchases occur. Convenience reduces hardship and is a key consideration in tax design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes should minimize excess burdens and administrative waste
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tax ought to be so contrived, as both to take out and to keep out of the pockets of the people as little as possible, over and above what it brings into the public treasury of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four identified channels of excess cost: (1) cost of collection (many officers' salaries/perquisites); (2) obstruction and discouragement of industry (discouraging desirable branches of business); (3) forfeitures and penalties from attempted evasion (ruining individuals, destroying beneficial capital use); (4) frequent intrusive examinations by tax-gatherers causing vexation equivalent to expense. Also warns taxes that tempt smuggling: law creates temptation then enhances punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer stable, permanent revenue sources over unstable credit-based funds
rubrics_metrics.description: The unstable and perishable nature of stock and credit, however, renders them unfit to be trusted to as the principal funds of that sure, steady, and permanent revenue, which can alone give security and dignity to government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper bills of credit, public stock, and credit may be expedients but are not reliable principal funds. Their success depends on demand, government credit, and moderation. Overuse produces disorder rather than convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land (rent) as a stable, principal source of public revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Land is a fund of more stable and permanent nature; and the rent of public lands, accordingly, has been the principal source of the public revenue of many a great nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: ancient Greek and Roman republics and ancient European sovereigns. But modern states' ordinary revenue often exceeds what land rent alone could provide; land rent's share of total revenue and its relation to household incomes are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/crown lands are an inefficient revenue source and better sold
rubrics_metrics.description: The revenue which, in any civilized monarchy, the crown derives from the crown lands, though it appears to cost nothing to individuals, in reality costs more to the society than perhaps any other equal revenue which the crown enjoys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: replace crown land revenue with an equal revenue and divide lands among the people, ideally by public sale; crown should retain lands for pleasure/magnificence only (parks, gardens, public walks). Sale proceeds could pay public debt and increase overall cultivation, population, consumption, and other tax receipts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish taxes by the fund they finally fall upon (rent/profit/wages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tax must finally be paid from some one or other of those three different sources of revenue, or from all of them indifferently (rent, profit, wages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter proposes analyzing taxes by which fund they are intended to fall upon (taxes on rent, on profit, on wages, or on all) because many taxes are not finally borne by the intended fund. This classification is essential for assessing equity and incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of a land tax: fixed valuation (invariable canon) vs. variable assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: A tax upon the rent of land may either be imposed according to a certain canon, every district being valued at a certain rent (invariable), or it may be imposed so as to vary with every variation in the real rent of the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed valuation advantages: certainty, convenience, low collection cost; but it becomes unequal over time as improvements/declensions occur. Variable assessment advantages: more equitable as rents change; disadvantages: greater administrative expense and potential uncertainty/oppression unless mitigated by proper registration and procedures. Trade-offs should be weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tax structures that discourage improvement of land
rubrics_metrics.description: A variable land-tax might discourage improvement because the sovereign would share in the profit of the landlord's improvement; landlords would be less disposed to improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations: allow landlord, before improvement, to ascertain valuation jointly with revenue officers and be rated according to that valuation for a number of years sufficient to indemnify him. The indemnification period should be long enough to compensate but not so long as to remove incentives for the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative safeguards to reduce uncertainty and fraud (registers, penalties, informer rewards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures like a public register of leases, penalties against concealing or misrepresenting lease terms, and rewards to informers are prescriptions to prevent collusion between lessor and lessee and to make assessments more certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording leases in public registers makes conditions known; penalties and informer rewards deter concealment. Equity and reduced uncertainty can be achieved without very high administrative cost if well designed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat fines for lease renewal and prescribed modes of cultivation as harmful practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Some landlords take a fine for renewal of lease or prescribe a mode of cultivation; these practices are often hurtful to tenant, landlord, and community and should be discouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fines for renewal sell future revenue for immediate ready money and drain tenant capital, reducing cultivation ability. Recommended responses: tax such fines heavier than ordinary rent; value prescribed cultivation conditions as additional (service) rent and tax accordingly to discourage them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer monetary rents over rents in kind or service; tax in-kind/service rents higher
rubrics_metrics.description: Rents in kind (corn, cattle, poultry, wine, oil) or in service are more hurtful to the tenant and less beneficial to the landlord and community than money-rents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such rents take or keep more of the tenant's productive capital or labor, they are associated with poverty among tenants. Valuing and taxing these species of rent higher can discourage their use and improve overall economic welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider local valuation/survey systems with periodic review for accurate assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states have used actual surveys and valuations of all lands, reviewed and altered from time to time, as a method of land-tax assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While more laborious and expensive than fixed valuation, surveys (e.g., Doomsday-book, Prussian valuations) can produce more accurate assessments. Expense must be balanced against benefits; a well-designed administrative system might moderate costs.
